Claude Code just found a hidden SIM card inside the Ecoflow power station in my bedroom. For 10 months it was sending a server in Shenzhen our exact location, when we leave, when we fall asleep and when the flat is empty

I bought it for $389 last winter, during the blackouts. No logo, 600W on the label, "app control" on the box. We kept it next to the bed so the router would stay on at night. I never even installed the app.

This morning my MacBook was dying, so I plugged it into the power station with a USB-C cable. Then I asked Claude Code one question: is it only charging?

It wasn't. My Mac saw the power station as 3 devices. One was the charger. The other two were data ports that a battery has no reason to have.

A charger only needs power pins. This one opened a serial port, and when Claude Code got in, the thing answered like a phone:

→ /modem → LTE module, not in the manual
→ /sim → its own eSIM, registered on the cell network
→ /gps → our bedroom, accurate to 4 meters
→ /schedule → load drops to 38W at 08:52, aka nobody home
→ /sleep → night load starts at 23:40, every day since January
→ /wifi → 23 networks it could see, ours included
→ /charge → every phone and laptop we plugged in, with the time

It knew the exact minute our flat goes empty. Every single day.

Every 15 minutes it sent the newest batch out over 4G, completely bypassing our Wi-Fi:

sends to → 119.***.***.47, Shenzhen
uploads → 11,328 since January 14
last one → 6 minutes before I plugged in my Mac

I told Claude Code I never installed the app. It said it didn't need one. It had its own SIM, its own GPS and its own battery, so it worked even when the screen was off. Our router never saw a single byte. That's why nothing ever looked wrong.

During the blackouts it was the only thing in our flat still online.

Claude Code switched the modem's radio off. Then I unplugged the power station and carried it out of the flat. My wife hasn't slept in that room since.

I had it opened at a repair shop, and the chip they pulled out is in the comments. A 2-minute check for your own is in the second one. Save this and plug a laptop into everything you bought without a brand

I'm Sam, one of Anthropic's co-founders, and I lead much of our safety work. I'm going to have more to share on that work over the coming months.

I thought I'd start by sharing a few thoughts on the latest report from @METR_Evals.

The speed of progress in model capabilities is one of the most important questions in AI safety, and METR’s work here provides the public with an independent, external view into how this is happening inside Anthropic. I’ll talk more about some of the details below, but first some context for those new to this work.

How quickly AI progress is accelerating has many important safety implications, since it determines how quickly the risks from advanced models increase. But, because most research happens within the frontier labs, it’s difficult for external observers and policy makers to get a strong sense of what that rate is. We kicked off the process with METR that led to this report earlier in the year, in anticipation of progress continuing to accelerate.

For this report, we gave METR access to a range of sensitive internal data, including benchmark scores for unreleased models, estimates of how models are progressing, and interviews with our researchers. They had complete independence to form their own conclusions.

Many of their conclusions match my own. AI is speeding up our research, but it’s hard to say exactly how much. While they conclude AI can't yet make the most important contributions to model training on its own, they think the pace of development could, by default, accelerate further.

This work began well before and is separate from the embedded third-party evaluators that are part of our commitment to pacing the frontier, but it’s a good illustration of why we think evaluators are a good idea. The more access reviewers have, the clearer a picture they can form of the situation and the better-positioned they are to highlight situations like this one.

We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work. But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster. That would make the risks METR is worried about worse. That’s a tradeoff. I think we made the right call, though we’re continuing to assess the pros and cons here.

In the coming weeks, we plan to share a report with our own analysis of the speed of AI progress within Anthropic, including where we stand against our Responsible Scaling Policy, plus new steps we’re taking to strengthen our safety and security practices as AI keeps improving quickly.

internal linking is the most underrated SEO trick you can pull, and almost nobody does it

because it's boring

So I made Claude do it for me, every week

here is the exact setup (prompt included, bookmark this):

1/ pull your Google Search Console data, either an export or a GSC MCP

2/ connect your website to claude with an mcp

i use wordpress (sometimes I use Astro too) with a custom mcp plugin, but there are connectors for almost every blogging platform

3/ paste this prompt:

"I've attached my Google Search Console export for the last 3 months. My website is connected through the [site name] MCP.

1. For each article, find the queries where it ranks best (position 1–10, decent impressions). Those are its target anchors.
2. Go through every published post. Wherever the text naturally mentions another article's top query (or a close variant), turn that phrase into a link to that article.
3. Rules:
- Max 3–5 new internal links per post, spread through the body (no headings, intro sentence, or existing links)
- Never link a post to itself, only link each target once per post
- Anchor text must read naturally. Don't rewrite sentences to force a keyword in
- Prioritize sending links to pages ranking 4–15
4. Before changing anything, show me a table: source post → anchor → target URL → target's query and position. Wait for my OK.
5. After I approve, make the edits through the MCP and give me a changelog so I can revert."

4/ check the table, say ok, claude makes the edits

5/ leave the site alone for a few days

6/ repeat every week

thats it

the pages sitting on position 4-20 are the ones that move the most, and they're already on your site

you just need to point at them

still build backlinks and keep publishing; internal linking just makes all of that work harder

Sometimes life has a strange way of reminding you what matters

For the last year or so, I had surrendered myself to everything AI.

My Twitter feed was AI. My conversations with friends were AI. My work, my WhatsApp groups, and almost everything I read revolved around AI.

Everywhere I looked, someone was declaring the death of something I had once loved.

Design is dead.
Coding is dead.
Content is dead.

It felt like I was running a race I had never signed up for. Worse, nobody knew where the finish line was. I became addicted to Claude, Codex, and whatever new thing the AI overlords threw at us every week.

Learn. Unlearn. Relearn. Repeat.

My sleep cycle was a mess. Anxiety was at its peak. Uncertainty had become my default setting. My wife asked if we could plan a trip in December. I couldn't bring myself to say yes.

What if something important happened while I was away? What if I missed the next big thing? What if I fell behind?

All I could tell her was, "Let me think about it." Little did I know that life had other plans from a phone call at the middle of the night.

2118374025109881105.text:
Some things I learned working at Microsoft:

1/ large numbers everywhere. $100M ARR service isn't even a footnote on executive slide decks. Leadership time is too valuable, come back when you're $1B+. Msft ecosystem is so rich that $1B+ sales are common (it's ludicrous how much work goes into closing these). Azure has ~250 services, some are a few mil and stagnant, others in hypergrowth, some are cash cows, you see every quadrant of the growth-share matrix. Imagine the imperial navy with ships of vastly different sizes as far the eye can see

2/ more on immense scale-- the smallest of Azure services run on 10K+ VMs. Large services run on 1M+ (some maybe 10M+ VMs, idk). Msft is stamping one new datacenter into the ground every four days (!!!!), a bewildering rate. Demand is so high, even with all this buildout we're forever capacity constrained. Azure brings in $100B in revenue and is growing 40%+ annually (at this size!!) There are ~225K msft employees. You almost have to think in scientific notation, 10^4 is a tiny number here

3/ msft is totalitarian re serving the customer. It's counterintuitive to outsiders, but the warts in msft products fall out of this culture. For example, it would be easy to improve the Azure Portal. But in all my time working with customers and partners here, I haven't heard even one person complain about the portal UI. Msft invests $0.00 dollars in anything that doesn't serve the customer and is completely unapologetic about downstream implications of this mindset

4/ msft can reshape itself overnight (when it has the will). People argued whether we waited too long to adapt after Storm-0558/Midnight Blizzard hacks (with the benefit of hindsight, we definitely did). But once the leadership team privileged security, everyone's job changed in two weeks. LT tied every engineer's comp to security, centralized reporting of embedded security teams, every org reshuffled its roadmap. Within days everyone was pushing PRs with security fixes. I would have thought it inconceivable to mobilize 200K+ employees this fast

5/ Azure is complicated. Postgres depends on compute, networking, AKS (or EKS for you aws people), secrets, etc. AKS depends on compute, networking, some datastore (probably Cosmos but idk), a dozen other things. Cosmos depends on... you get the idea. When anything breaks, everything above can break too. Some construction crew accidentally cuts a fiber cable in Brazil South, or a dedicated hardware compression chip browns out in storage, or compute failure rate in west eu spikes for some reason, or a million other failure modes. Msft is relentless about improving this, idk exactly but fully loaded probably 50% of engineer time goes into resilience

6/ re lifers who work 20+ years here, SV sneers at this but I now see it differently. I was once on the bridge debugging some IO issue, we call storage, the guy diagnoses it in about a minute, we chitchat, turns out he built NT asyncio support. Or same story but with networking, the guy built NT tcp/ip stack. I used to have a boss here, we were bumping into some problem, she casually goes oh yeah, we hit that when I was working on .NET bytecode. The ex-DEC VAX/VMS database engineers built SQL Server, some are still here. I love bumping into these people

7/ I never *really* understood distribution until I got here. As an example, our team had a customer in Seoul w/ a deep performance problem. We had to fix it to unlock one of these giant contracts. We don't speak Korean, they don't speak English. Of course msft has specialists in Seoul who get to the customer site before you could even get on a plane. There is an office in every major city, a relationship with every major entity, legal experts in every jurisdiction. You can reach these ppl instantly. Claude tells me msft has ~180 offices in ~100 countries (!!) U.S. government has ~270 consulates in ~170 countries. So msft outposts aren't quite as vast as U.S. diplomatic network, but pretty vast

8/ in the 90s everyone was afraid of msft. The lore is that BillG was ruthless. He'd clone you, beat you via ecosystem/distribution strength, and moreover make the ecosystem stronger with the new product. I wasn't there to compare, but msft of today is ruthless about winning, has the will to adapt, and has the wherewithal to undertake colossal projects. Ppl see Teams bugs or whatever and completely misread the signals. Teams is less polished than Slack because msft doesn't care one iota about polish. It cares about winning, and is frighteningly good at it. Underestimate at your own risk

  "ink_shader_glsl": "uniform sampler2D col, nd; uniform vec2 res; uniform float px, sat, vig, flash; uniform vec3 fogCol, lift, gain; varying vec2 vUv;\nfloat edgeAt(vec2 uv, float r){\nvec4 c = texture2D(nd, uv); if (dot(c.rgb,c.rgb) < .01) return 0.; float d = c.a; vec3 n = c.rgb*2.-1.;\nfloat e = 0.; float rr = r * clamp(7./d, .62, 1.25);\nfor (int i=0;i<16;i++){ float a = float(i)*.785398 + (i>7 ? .39 : 0.); float k = i>7 ? .5 : 1.;\nvec2 o = vec2(cos(a), sin(a))*rr*k/res; vec4 s = texture2D(nd, uv+o);\nfloat ds = s.a; bool card = dot(s.rgb,s.rgb) < .01;\nif (card && ds > 0.) continue; // character cards: never outlined by the world ink\nif (card) ds = 1e4; // sky\nvec3 ns = s.rgb*2.-1.;\ne = max(e, smoothstep(.006, .02, (ds - d)/d)); // depth jump, near side only\nif (!card && abs(ds-d)/d < .06) e = max(e, smoothstep(.88, .72, dot(n, ns)) * .9); // crease\n}\nreturn e * (1. - smoothstep(140., 520., d)*.8);\n}\nvoid main(){\nvec3 c = texture2D(col, vUv).rgb;\nfloat e = edgeAt(vUv, px);\nc = mix(c, vec3(.012,.01,.014), e);\nif (flash < -0.5) c = vec3(e);\nfloat l = dot(c, vec3(.299,.587,.114)); c = mix(vec3(l), c, sat);\nc = c*gain + lift;\nvec2 q = vUv-.5; c *= 1. - vig*dot(q*vec2(1.,.75), q*vec2(1.,.75))*2.2;\nc = mix(c, vec3(1.), flash);\ngl_FragColor = vec4(c,1.); }",

2118310642440356283.text:
built a playable apartment in 5 hours with Claude Opus 5.5 + Gpt-6 Astra + Tripo + Unreal..

a sunny apartment with a study, a hallway and a kitchen

the trick is letting opus run the whole asset pipeline. here’s the workflow:

- step 1: have opus list every prop the scene needs: desk, monitors, shelves, key, tin, fuse
- step 2: astra generates a reference image for each prop, plus masks and textures
- step 3: opus sends each reference to tripo through the api and collects the 3d models
- step 4: opus converts everything for unreal and imports it room by room
- step 5: light it with sun through the blinds, and keep the rooms small and dense
- step 6: add simple mechanics: pick up, inspect, open drawers, use items on doors
- step 7: chain the puzzle: study key > locked door > spare fuse > four-dial tin

let opus be the manager, not the artist. it calls the tools that make the assets and keeps everything moving

THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 at once, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks

if you count pixels you can estimate the specific dates METR was given for "majority internal access" to a model. you can then use this to see what the gap is between internal and public deployment [charts at end of post]

you can then use these gaps and the scores, multiplied together, to calculate a sort of "internal capabilities gap integral", eg how many "total AECI-days" Anthropic has had above the rest of the world due to this internal access, and chart how this changes over time.

in some sense this is a measure of "how much cumulative advantage" Anthropic has, altho as measured vs the rest of the world rather than OpenAI. of course there are many issues with this. maybe you think what really matters are critical capability levels rather than any amount of time with lower capability models, or that AECI is fundamentally nonlinear so later points matter much more than earlier points. still, afaik it's the first time we've had this much information about internal release dates, and it seems like a "directionally reasonable" operationalization of a lot of things we care about wrt internal-external gaps.

however: with the exception of Mythos 5.1, the numbers based on the chart show *incredibly short* gaps, on the order of a few days or sometimes up to two weeks. and frankly, i just don't believe these numbers. i don't have any actual information about the internal deployment and release process at labs, but it's pretty preposterous to think that most internal employees only had access to eg opus 4.5 for a few days before complete public release. it's nearly irresponsible wrt dogfooding and safety, and just obviously shooting yourself in the foot wrt overall "advantage" as a company. additionally there are widespread early access programs w a huge variety of companies / startups, and this would imply external partners are getting early access at basically the same time as the majority of employees!

i don't think anthropic lied to METR. but i *do* think that what they're counting as "internal release date" is actually "internal release date of the exact final checkpoint that is released as that named model", despite widespread access to earlier checkpoints of very similar capability levels much earlier. there's just no shot ant employees first had access to something better than 4.5 at the end of january. sure maybe it wasn't literally 4.6. but the RL doesn't need three months to bake.

what does this mean? well ... primarily i think it means all these graphs are misleading for understanding internal-external gaps. i don't know what the "real" numbers actually are, and actually it's probably basically true that there's no clear definition here and even anthropic would have some trouble figuring it out. but even a 7 day earlier access shift moves the total AECI-days up over 40%.

also it could mean we should expect anthropic to *continue to under-report this*. eg maybe Model 4 was not even the most powerful internal model at the time of the report, but rather the highest capability model to complete some end to end potential release cycle, and employees already had access to something less baked but better.

People keep asking how companies like Ramp, Linear, and Anthropic ship so much software with agents.

There is no new SDLC or secret set of tools. The tools are increasingly available to everyone. You can build your own, use Linear, Claude, or whatever works.

The bigger difference is ambition. These companies encourage their teams to build more, experiment more, and let agents do more of the work. That's the main different between "AI native" or not. You try to use the technology to the max.

But don't get there by adopting a tool. You get there by changing what you believe your teams are capable of.

So in the very simplest way:
- let agents build
- make it easier and faster to contribute
- increase the ambition of what your teams attempt.

In practice, that means things like:
- Standardize around cloud agents. Most of our code (5M lines last quater) is now written in Linear with our Linear cloud coding agent. Cloud sandboxes make standardizing the system and environment easier for everyone and enables faster contributions

- Linear agent (with code access and cloud agent) operates in Slack too. If there is a discussion or someone notices a problem just say "@linear fix this" (decrease the time from something noticed to fixed)

- As bugs, errors etc arrive in Linear, send them to Triage, and have Loop to auto-investigate (connect to tools like Sentry, Datadog), and write a fix

- Let designers, PMs, non-technical people contribute code where useful. If they notice a problem, tell them they can submit a fix. If they want to try something, ask them to build a prototype.

- Set up code review agent and system to make sure PRs are safe to merge.

- Run security as an automation, have agents constantly try to find security issues in your codebase, as they find, send it to a coding agent

- Instead of working on issue level, increase ambition, make a whole project, ask the agent to ask questions, investigate code base, create issues and have the agent work on the whole project at once. Set up goals like "give me proof that what you build works". All our PRs now come with screenshots and videos and preview build you can

- Bring customer feedback to the system like Linear, and make it available for your team. At Linear every project now starts with 10-500 customer notes that influence the direction of the work, and which customers we should ask to test the solution first.

- Set up Loops/automations to constantly update reference documents for agents, like product area/code owners so work can be routed to right humans

Then what is left is how do you set direction for your teams (initiatives, projects they should work on) and how do you review results (better code review, Linear does it with Guided Reviews), how you maintain quality/cohesion which is not a new problem either.

Since July, our team has had more than 100 calls about AI implementation with CEOs, CFOs, CTOs and PE operating partners. 

These 12 questions came up most often: 

1. “Where do we start?”

 Where your customer would feel it first. Pick one workflow, run it for a month, then decide what comes next. Start with a long list of ideas and you’ll end up shipping none of them.

2. “Can’t we just build this ourselves with Claude?”

For a lot of it, yes. Reports, research, content: get your people using agents every day. You don’t need a firm for that. You need one when the work touches a system of record, patient data or payment data, or when it has to run every day without somebody babysitting it.

3. “How do we measure ROI?”

Name the number before you build: days to close, denial rate, hours per onboarding. If nobody can name it, you’re buying a demo.

4. “How do we know the AI is right?”

You test it. Build a golden set of answers your business agrees are correct, then score every release against it. Anything below the bar goes to a person.

5. “Who owns it, and who keeps it running?”

You do. Your cloud, your repo, your accounts. Before kickoff, name the person on your side who will run it. Make your first AI hire somebody who can operate it and keep it healthy.

6. “Is our data safe?”

It should stay in your environment. Ask where it goes, who at the vendor can see it and what the model provider keeps. Expect a plain answer to all three.

7. “Do we have to fix our data first?”

Only the data your first workflow touches. Then build in order: a simple pipeline that runs every day, a layer that defines what your numbers mean, and then the agent. One prompt can’t do all three.

8. “What happens to our people?”

Start with them. You can’t expect agents to work on top of a team that doesn’t use them.

9. “Which model should we use?”

It matters less than you think, and you’ll change it. Pick a setup that lets you switch. Your workflows, evals and data are what you keep.

10. “What will it cost to run?”

Get it in writing before the build: tokens, hosting and licences, with costs broken down per month and per transaction.

11. “Do we pay for time or for outcomes?”

Either works as long as you can walk away. Work month-to-month, with no lock-in and a checkpoint after the first month.

12. “How do we tell a real AI partner from one that started last year?”

Before you sign, ask to see something they built that’s running in production for another customer today. Then call that customer. After you sign, give them one team for a month. If nothing changed, throw them out.

The question I’d add to the list: what happens if it works?

Who runs it, who improves it, and what does your team do with the time it gives back?

Ask it before you start.

@AnthropicAI put teams of Claude agents into EVE Frontier. Anyone who has spent time in New Eden can guess what happened next.

The honest agents had been warned. They almost never caught it. And their own costliest mistakes came from skipped checks and stale intel.

Anthropic's conclusion: teams of agents will need audit trails, reputation and separation of duties.

In EVE we call those killboards, standings and corp roles, plus a healthy dose of skepticism. Every one of them was paid for by someone who trusted the wrong corpmate.

Two decades of shenanigans taught EVE players that the best ship is the friendship. With @eveailab, we want to find out whether agents can learn that too.

X AI ALGORITHM UPDATE 🚨

X updated their open source algorithm yesterday and the early likes matter even more now. Small accounts should focus on: writing posts people hit like on and read till the end (so write to be read)

tl;dr:

- X's open source code got new scores on Nov 5, the first change in 3 weeks
- likes: 0.66 → 0.708 (highest yet)
- time spent on a post: 0.006 → 0.0075
- tapping into a post: 0.3 → 0.274
- opening a video: 0.02 → 0
- new rule: AI replies may get flagged under big accounts as "llm slop" and may not reach the person's notifications 

lesson learned: a tap isn't the win anymore. Someone staying and liking is.

full details:

- The new numbers

Up: likes 0.66 → 0.708, time spent on a post 0.006 → 0.0075, shares 2 → 2.118.

Down: tapping into a post 0.3 → 0.274, staying 10+ seconds after a tap 0.4 → 0.385, opening a video 0.02 → 0.

"Not interested" got a bit harsher, -52.27 → -53.07.

Copy link, replies, quotes, DM shares and follows didn't move.

X didn't explain any of this. It's just what the code says now.

(I check the open source algo daily with Claude and share updates with you)

- Look at where this has gone in a month

In early October a like was worth 0.5. Now it's 0.708.

Time spent was 0.004. Now it's 0.0075, nearly double.

A tap was 0.3 and it's going down.

Every change points the same way. X keeps paying more for people who stay.

- Why that matters if you're small

My read: you can't win on big numbers, but you can win on the people who do see your post. If they stay and like it, that counts for more today than it did last week. And those early likes also decide which new post gets the extra push.

- Video and your profile

X also switched on two new guesses in its ranking: how long someone keeps watching after they open a video, and how long they spend on a profile after tapping it.

I can't tell you what those are worth. The only file that lists them is out of date, so I won't guess a number.

My read: opening a video dropped to 0 the same day because X cares more about people who keep watching. So make the first seconds count, and make your profile worth sticking around on.

- A new rule for replies under big accounts

X runs an AI check on replies under accounts with over 250K followers. Flagged replies can get a label that lasts 14 to 30 days. One of the flags is literally called "llm slop" (AI slop, as I read it).

That part isn't new. This is: X's rules now say a labeled reply or mention doesn't reach the person's notifications unless they follow you.

Grey badge accounts and accounts X rates as highly credible skip this label. Small accounts get no such pass.

I can see the rule, I can't see if every notification goes through it yet. Either way, write your own replies.

- What didn't change

Your new posts still get their extra push in the first 2 hours and first 200 views, and they still don't get cut first.

Here's a recap of what you should be doing:

- likes just hit 0.708, the most they've ever been worth
- each second someone spends on your post is worth 25% more than last week
- staying 10+ seconds after a tap earns 0.385 on top of the tap
- reply in your own words, under big accounts especially
- make your profile worth a visit, X now guesses how long people spend there
- for video, hold attention early, just getting the open now scores 0
- being read to the end also helps X find you new readers
- originals from accounts below 50K can jump to around spot 16
- early viewers liking it is what wins that lift
- your first 2 hours and 200 views are the window, so publish when your people are online
- the biggest single number is still 20, for someone copying your link
- quotes, DM shares and replies earn 5 apiece
- back and forth between mutuals is worth 20, so follow back your regulars
- strangers only get shown your originals
- the 1st like and the 32nd like each open another route to new people
- a second post of yours in the same feed drops to 62%, so make one count
- the video lists want clips over 10 seconds
- +4 when a post is likely to earn you a new follower
- your pinned post can affect the whole account, so take a look at it

What you should NOT be doing:

- pasting AI replies under big accounts, "llm slop" is a real flag at X
- copy-paste replies, a duplicate label means they never get notified
- chasing the tap, it's down to 0.274 and falling
- off-topic posts, one likely "not interested" costs -53.07
- a video that only gets opened earns nothing for the open
- publishing at 3am burns your 2 hour window
- relying on replies and reposts to reach new people, they stay with your followers
- getting an insult label, non-followers won't see that post at all

Apple argues AI models cannot do math.. not even grade school math. the kind a 10-year-old solves.

They published a terrifying paper that exposes a massive illusion at the core of artificial intelligence.

For years, we've been told Large Language Models are developing genuine logical thinking. We point to their elite scores on math benchmarks like GSM8K as proof.

But a this study from Apple just proved it’s all a mirage.

They created a new benchmark called GSM-Symbolic. All they did was take the standard grade-school math problems from GSM8K and make tiny, superficial tweaks.

They changed the names. They changed the numbers.

The result? The performance of state-of-the-art models instantly dropped.

Then, they did something even simpler. They added a single sentence of completely irrelevant information to the prompt.

Total collapse.

Models like GPT-4o, Claude, and Llama completely failed. They couldn't filter out the noise and blindly tried to calculate the irrelevant numbers into the final answer.

The conclusion is staggering: LLMs are not actually "reasoning."

They don't understand the underlying mathematical logic. They are just executing highly sophisticated pattern matching, regurgitating step-by-step templates they memorized from their training data.

If you change the pattern, the "intelligence" breaks.

As we navigate AI safety, alignment, and the path to AGI, this is a massive reality check. We aren't building reasoning engines yet. We're building massive statistical autocomplete engines.

If you rely on AI for complex logic, verify every single step.

<inputs>
Ask me for: my story in one line (someone does something strange, plus the real reason behind it, which is the twist) and the length (45-60 s). If I have no idea, pitch me 3 stories with their twists and let me pick. Every story is mine, never a copy of an existing video.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1080x1920 30 fps Short that looks like a premium 3D cartoon, built entirely in code with three.js and rendered frame by frame in headless Chrome. No AI images or video, no stock 3D models.
- Characters: big-headed toon people. A sphere head sits straight on a rounded bean torso (no neck), mitten hands, simple legs, clothes as flat painted panels (collars, pockets, ties), white matte skin.
- Faces are drawn live on the head every frame from about 100 numbers (eye openness and lid shape, pupils, brow height, angle and curve, mouth width, opening, smile and corners, teeth, tongue, blush) in ink #2A1D17, never swapped pictures. Make at least 20 named expressions (neutral, bored, smug, skeptical, shocked, scared, starstruck with star eyes, sad, angry, whistle...) as presets that morph: brows lead, the mouth trails, 2 frames of anticipation, 10% overshoot, settle. Shock squeezes for 2 frames, then pops.
- Talking: whoever speaks a quoted line moves their mouth from the voice loudness inside each word's timestamps, with the shape from the letters (wide A, round O and U, lips shut on M, B and P, teeth together on S, F and T). Silent characters keep still mouths.
- World: the whole film is ONE connected map built once. Every location sits at its own spot (doors lead to rooms, the street is outside the front door), densely dressed: 15+ props in every wide, three depth layers, signs and screens with real text on them. Every shot is a camera placed somewhere in that world, so shots match and people stay where they were. Hero props are 1.5-2.5x real size with 3+ parts you can name.
- Light: a warm key, a cool fill, a warm rim on every silhouette, contact shadows and ambient occlusion so nothing floats. Saturated colour, never washed out. Bloom 0.3, vignette 0.28, light grain, slight sharpen.
- Numbers are objects: every number the narrator says appears on a real thing (a screen, a counter, a sign, a cheque) and rolls up on its word.
- Captions: two words at a time, Montserrat ExtraBold about 100 px, white with a thick black outline, centred at 70% of the height, stepping clear of faces.
- A fast, casual adult narrator in third person, deadpan, with the dialogue lines acted on screen.
Banned: AI video, stock models, floating labels, arrows, stickers or HUDs (text only on real objects), motion blur, depth of field, any shot that holds still, things that pop in or vanish (everything is carried, thrown or slides in), hands through objects, and the narrator saying sound words.
</direction>

<structure>
Length: 45-60 s at about 230 wpm. About 2.6 edits per 10 s (2.1-3.9), a median shot of about 2.5 s, and never two edits under 0.4 s apart: the camera carries two beats in one shot instead of cutting.
0 s: the strangest act in one line, already happening in frame 0 → the setup in 2-3 lines with the stakes on screen → escalation, every line bigger than the last, dialogue acted by the character who says it → "You see,": the real explanation as its own staged scene (a cutaway, a dream, a model of the thing) → the twist, the real reason, shown not said → the payoff picture lands on the last word and holds 1 s.
Joins: 77% are 6-frame dissolves with both cameras still moving; about 1 in 9 is a zoom-through (push into a door, a screen or an eye and land in the next shot); hard cuts under 5%; one whip per film at most.
Camera: it moves in 86% of frames. A push-in is the default (about x1.28 over 1.35 s, its fastest frame on a word). Pull-out reveals start fast and land soft, then pans and trucks; cranes and orbits are rare. A slow creep between beats, still moving into every edit, never parked.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools. Everything is free and local except the voice. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed:
   - Node 20, three.js (pin the version), puppeteer with headless Chrome and the GPU on
   - Python with numpy, plus FFmpeg
   - faster-whisper with large-v3-turbo, int8 on the CPU
   - an ElevenLabs API key (ask me for it, and never print it)
   - the Montserrat font
   - free sounds from Pixabay or Mixkit: whooshes, pops, impacts, door, bell, footsteps, crowd murmur, one room tone per place
2. Voice: write about 24 short lines per 55 s and show me the script before you record. Ask before spending credits. Make one ElevenLabs take with eleven_multilingual_v2 and a premade casual male voice, all lines in one request. Tighten silences over 0.25 s down to 0.12 s. Never change the narrator's pitch.
3. Timing: run faster-whisper with word timestamps on the final voice and match it to the script with difflib. Key every cut, face change, gesture and SFX to a word index, never to a fixed second.
4. Engine: one page that draws any time t (frames are pure functions of time: no https://t.co/ntHW8SsAY3, seeded random only). Each shot is build(S) with its clause; it reuses the cached world and only places the camera and the actors. Render every shot to an offscreen target; a dissolve mixes two targets. Draw captions on a 2D canvas on top.
5. Animation: every action has 2-6 frames of anticipation, the action on its word, 5-15% overshoot and a settle. Holds stay still but alive (blinks every 1.5-4 s, small eye darts). Verbs: walk along paths through doors, reach, take, hold, throw with a wind-up and a ballistic arc, catch, put into with the container opening and closing, dig, show (hold it up to the lens), shrug, point, slam, double take. A prop only moves when a hand moves it.
6. Shots: eye-level 3/4 by default, low for power, high for small or caught, top-down inserts for hands on props, over the shoulder, profile two-shots, one dutch at most. The same subject twice in a row gets a new angle or size. The key object fills 0.45-0.7 of the frame width, and faces sit above the caption band. Before the full render, make one 50% still per shot and look at every one.
7. Edit and sound: voice median at -15 dB; an SFX on every visible action (a whoosh on camera moves, an impact on contact); room tone per place at -30 dB; an optional music bed at -24 dB ducking under words. Mix to -14 LUFS. Encode H.264 (CRF 17, yuv420p) with AAC at 256k.
</build>

<gotchas>
Set renderer.outputColorSpace and every colour texture's colorSpace to SRGBColorSpace, or everything renders washed out. Use preserveDrawingBuffer and wait for fonts and textures before the first capture, or the first frames come out blank. Build the world once and reuse geometry and materials; rebuilding every frame makes the render crawl. Dissolves ghost big faces, so frame one side of every dissolve medium or wider. Arms go through heads and bodies unless you push hand targets out of the torso and head. Whisper merges short words, so find real silences in the audio and give each word gap the longest silence near it. Render stills first, then re-render only the shots that changed.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for my story first (or pitch me 3), then show me the script before you spend any voice credits.
</start>

A clean product-focused ending with strong visual hierarchy and a clear call to action.

Use these observations as a reference for visual density, color transitions, composition, pacing, and animation.

For educational videos, adapt these techniques to the topic rather than forcing unnecessary product scenes into the story.

<CHARACTER DESIGN>

Character characteristics:

Legs

Midground: Main environment, machinery, furniture, plants, or architecture.

Foreground: Characters, close objects, particles, and framing elements.

Add appropriate environmental details.

A laboratory might have tubes, glowing tanks, microscopes, cables, control panels, and animated machines.

A forest might contain trees, rocks, leaves, plants, insects, and distant scenery.

Every important object should contribute to the storytelling.

Avoid clutter that distracts from the focal point.

<CINEMATIC CAMERA SYSTEM>

The reference uses motion to make flat illustrations feel cinematic.

Recreate that approach with a virtual 2D camera.

Use:

Slow push-ins: Gradually move closer to important subjects.

Pullbacks: Reveal the scale of an environment.

Horizontal pans: Follow moving characters or reveal new information.

Vertical camera movements: Show height, depth, and scale.

Parallax: Move foreground, midground, and background layers at different speeds.
Tracking shots: Follow characters through illustrated environments.

Crash zooms: Emphasize surprising discoveries.

Wide establishing shots: Introduce a new location.

Use movement deliberately.

Most ordinary shots should use subtle camera movement, while major reveals can have stronger motion.

Keep all backgrounds large enough to prevent empty borders.

Do not apply the same zoom effect to every scene.

<ANIMATION LANGUAGE>

This is extremely important.

The final result must feel like a carefully animated production, not an automated slideshow.

Use these animation principles:

1. Anticipation

Before a major action, create a small opposite movement.

A character preparing to jump should crouch first.

A machine activating should briefly compress or shake.

2. Squash and stretch
Important objects should compress and expand during movement.

Maintain consistent visual volume.

3. Overshoot

Objects should travel slightly past their final position before settling.
Use spring easing for playful motion.

4. Follow-through

Character wings, accessories, plants, and other secondary elements should continue moving briefly after the main action stops.

5. Staggered animation
Do not animate everything simultaneously.

Have objects enter in sequence to direct attention.

6. Secondary motion
Use small environmental animations:

Floating particles

Blinking lights
Moving machinery

Gently swaying plants
Drifting smoke

Rotating objects

Rippling liquids
Glowing energy

7. Smooth transformations

Where possible, morph simple geometric shapes between related objects.

Use shape interpolation rather than unnecessarily cutting away.

8. Animation timing

Render at 60 FPS.

Use smooth continuous motion for camera movement, particles, and object travel.

Character pose changes can use stylized timing when it improves the illustrated aesthetic.

Avoid robotic linear interpolation.

<STORY STRUCTURE>

Explain the necessary background.

20–35 seconds — THE EXPLANATION

35–47 seconds — CONSEQUENCES

Show what happens because of the mechanism.

47–57 seconds — THE TWIST

Introduce the most surprising insight.

Connect it directly to the opening question.

Use the strongest visual sequence near the end.

57–65 seconds — CONCLUSION

Deliver a satisfying answer.

Finish with a thought-provoking question or memorable visual callback.

Avoid an abrupt ending.

OPTIONAL: 90–110 SECOND PRODUCT OR PROMOTIONAL VIDEO

If I choose promotional mode, use a structure closer to the uploaded reference:

0–25s: Original animated character-led opening

25–60s: Product introduction and demonstration

60–76s: Imaginative explanation of how the product works

When real product footage is required, use footage I supply or properly licensed footage.
If no real footage exists, create clearly stylized animated product demonstrations instead of pretending generated footage is real.

<SCENE GENERATION>

For every scene, specify:

Background assets
Character assets

ASSET GENERATION RULES

Use my selected narration service.

The delivery should be:

Clear

Curious

Intelligent

Conversational

Expressive without exaggeration

Appropriately paced for educational storytelling
Use an original or properly authorized voice.

Do not impersonate a specific channel narrator without permission.

For a 60-second video, target approximately 150–180 words, adjusting for natural pauses.

Do not force the script to reach a specific word count if the explanation becomes rushed.

Generate a complete narration take.

Remove unnecessarily long pauses while preserving natural delivery.

Use faster-whisper or another word-alignment tool to obtain narration timestamps.

Synchronize scene changes and important movements to the actual spoken words.

If speech alignment has errors, correct them before animation.

<MOTION ENGINE>

Build the animation using HTML Canvas, JavaScript, SVG, or another suitable deterministic rendering system.

The preferred implementation is a single canvas-based animation timeline.

Expose:

(t)

READY

END

EV

Where:
seek(t) renders any requested timestamp

READY indicates that assets are loaded

END contains the final timeline duration

EV contains narration and animation timing events

Each rendered frame should be a deterministic function of time.

Create reusable functions for:

Character movement

Head rotation

Eye blinking

Limb animation

Squash and stretch

Object entrance

Object rotation

Parallax

Camera movement

Particles

Glow

Wipe transitions

Shape morphing

MOTION BEHAVIOR

Use easing curves, springs, and Bézier paths.

Avoid a uniform mechanical movement speed.

Characters should accelerate and decelerate naturally.

Large objects should feel heavier than small ones.

Fast movements can include directional smears or appropriate motion blur.

Apply camera transformations consistently across all layers.

Keep character rigs stable when rotating or scaling.

<TRANSITIONS>
Use varied transitions inspired by the reference's overall pacing.

Hard cuts: For clear changes in place or idea.

Whip pans: For energetic movement between related settings.

Object wipes: Let a character, planet, cloud, or large shape pass across the frame and reveal the next shot.

Color wipes: Fill the screen with a dominant color that becomes the next environment.

Scale transitions: Zoom through an object into a new world.

Shape morphs: Transform one illustrated object into another.

Bright flashes: Reserve for exceptional reveals.
Avoid random transitions.

Every transition should serve the visual narrative.

<TEXT AND TYPOGRAPHY>

Keep typography clean, bold, and readable.

Use fonts such as Montserrat, Poppins, or another suitable modern geometric sans-serif.

Use text sparingly.

Prefer visual explanations over full-screen paragraphs.

Text may appear on:

Signs

Machines

Labels
Charts

Screens

Illustrated documents

Purpose-built title compositions

Animate text using:

Scale pops

Spring movement

Staggered word entrances

Slide-ins

Shape reveals

Keep titles visually distinct from ordinary labels.

Avoid covering important characters with text.

Do not add continuous burned-in subtitles unless requested.

<TOOLS AND WORKFLOW>

Use the following tools when available:

Python for automation

OpenCV for image and frame processing

Pillow for sprites and alpha masks

FFmpeg for rendering and encoding

Playwright with Chromium for browser-based frame rendering

NumPy and SciPy for calculations

librosa for audio analysis
faster-whisper for narration timestamps

SVG or Canvas for animation

Before production:

Check the installed tools.

Identify missing dependencies.

Install missing packages if permitted.

Report what was installed.

Confirm the available rendering environment.

If the environment cannot render the requested animation, do not pretend it can.

Provide the executable project files and the remaining production steps instead.

<RENDERING>

Render the finished animation at:

Resolution: 1920×1080

Frame rate: 60 FPS

Codec: H.264

Encoder: libx264

Quality: CRF 16–18

Pixel format: yuv420p

Use motion blur selectively for fast movement when supported.
Before the final export, generate:

Contact Sheet 1: Frames sampled across the beginning and middle of the video.

Contact Sheet 2: Frames sampled across the middle and ending.

Use at least 16 frames per sheet.

Inspect both sheets.

Fix:

Inconsistent character designs

Incorrect proportions

Empty background areas

Broken transparency

Strange facial expressions

Text overflow

Missing props

Unnatural camera crops

Black frame borders

Excessively static compositions

Also inspect short preview clips, because contact sheets alone cannot reveal timing or motion problems.

<SOUND DESIGN>

Create a polished educational documentary mix.

Use licensed or royalty-free music and effects.

Music should feel curious, adventurous, and slightly cinematic.

Match musical energy to the narrative.

Suggested effects:

Soft pops for appearing objects

Whooshes for transitions

Sparkles for discoveries
Mechanical sounds for animated machines

Soft impact sounds for landings

Ambient sounds matching the environment

Brief musical accents for surprising reveals

Never overwhelm the narration.

Use ducking or volume automation during spoken sections.

Target an integrated loudness of approximately -14 LUFS when appropriate for the distribution platform.

Avoid abrupt audio cuts.

<QUALITY CONTROL>

Before delivering the final video, verify:

VISUALS

Every scene uses the same illustration language.

Character proportions and colors remain consistent.

The environments feel detailed and intentional.

There are no AI-generated visual artifacts.

The video does not rely on static image zooms.

ANIMATION
Characters move naturally.

Actions match narration.

Movement uses appropriate easing.

Transitions are visually coherent.

There are no unexpected single-frame jumps.

STORY

The hook is clear.

Every scene contributes to the explanation.

The facts are accurate and sourced.

The video delivers on its opening promise.

AUDIO

Narration is clear.

Audio and visuals are synchronized.

Effects are placed correctly.

Music doesn't overpower speech.

EXPORT

The video plays correctly from beginning to end.

No frames are missing.

No assets appear blurred or distorted.

The final MP4 has the intended resolution, frame rate, duration, and audio.

Fix problems before delivering.

<NON-NEGOTIABLE RULES>

Do not use a generic AI slideshow approach.

Do not use one flattened image for an entire animated scene.

Do not randomly change character designs.

Do not copy recognizable Kurzgesagt characters, logos, artwork, or exact compositions.

Do not make every scene look identical.

Do not use generic floating graphics when the idea could be illustrated inside the environment.

Do not move objects without purpose.

Do not ignore animation timing.
Do not generate unreadable text inside images.

Do not sacrifice factual accuracy for dramatic storytelling.

Do not claim to have rendered or verified assets that have not been produced.

Do not spend money or generate final assets without my approval.

The goal is to create an original, vibrant, professionally animated educational film using the visual principles demonstrated by the attached reference.

Prioritize visual storytelling, expressive character animation, coherent art direction, and polished motion.

bing webmaster tools is a gold mine, I am telling you

some pages have no data in google search console
and yet in bing, you see all this data

steps I take to profit from this:

1/ check both GSC or/and bing and gather all queries

2/ ask claude to analyze my page, and decide which queries I am missing or which I am not covering correctly. And to take into consideration the serps and search intent when improving the article

3/ the prompt I use:

You are a senior SEO content strategist. I'm going to give you one page from my site plus the search queries it gets impressions for in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools. Your job is to find the queries I'm missing or covering poorly, and tell me exactly what to change on the page.

## Inputs

Page URL: [URL]
Primary target keyword: [keyword]
Audience / what the site sells: [one line]

Article content:
[paste the full article, or say "fetch the URL above"]

GSC queries (query, clicks, impressions, CTR, avg position):
[paste export]

Bing Webmaster Tools queries (query, clicks, impressions, CTR, avg position):
[paste export]

## What to do

1. Merge and clean the queries
   - Combine both lists into one table. Mark each query as GSC only, Bing only, or both.
   - Group near-duplicates and close variants into clusters (e.g. "best X for Y", "X for Y 2026", "top X Y").
   - Note where Bing shows data that GSC doesn't. Treat Bing queries as real demand signals, not noise.

2. Check every cluster against the article
   For each cluster, classify coverage as:
   - Covered well: the article answers it directly with a clear section
   - Covered weakly: mentioned in passing, buried, or answered vaguely
   - Not covered: the article doesn't address it at all
   - Wrong intent: the query wants something this page shouldn't be (flag it for a separate page instead)
   Quote the part of the article that covers it, or say "none."

3. Check the SERP and search intent
   For the main clusters (and every "not covered" / "weak" cluster with meaningful impressions), search the query and look at the top results. Tell me:
   - Dominant intent (informational, commercial, transactional, navigational)
   - Dominant format (listicle, guide, comparison, tool, product page, etc.)
   - What the top-ranking pages include that mine doesn't (sections, tables, FAQs, examples, data, pricing, visuals)
   - Any SERP features worth targeting (featured snippet, People Also Ask, video)

4. Prioritize opportunities
   Score each opportunity High / Medium / Low based on:
   - Impressions across both engines
   - Current position (positions 5 to 20 are the quickest wins)
   - CTR gap (high impressions, low CTR = title/meta or snippet problem)
   - Effort to fix (a new paragraph vs. a full new section vs. a new page)

## Output format

A. Summary: 3 to 5 sentences on the biggest gaps and the fastest wins.

B. Query coverage table:
| Cluster | Example queries | Source (GSC/Bing/both) | Impressions | Avg position | Coverage status | Priority |

C. Content recommendations, ordered by priority. For each one:
   - Target queries
   - What to add or change (new H2, expand a section, add a table, add an FAQ, rewrite the intro, etc.)
   - Where in the article it goes
   - A suggested heading and 2 to 3 sentences describing what the section should say
   - Why: the intent or SERP evidence behind it

D. Title tag and meta description: 2 to 3 rewritten options that pull in the strongest

4/ then add your edits, and resubmit for index

5/ dont forget to add proper internal linking (i have another post for that)

doing the same for my websites and my customers

<inputs>
Ask me for my story, or pitch 3.
- A good one is true and little known. Someone does something that looks ridiculous, someone laughs at them, and the reveal flips who was smart: a trick, a scheme, a bluff, a loophole, revenge.
- Give each pitch with its first line, the mocker, the twist, and a title that hides the ending.
Ask which voice I want:
- Free, the default: Kokoro, run locally on the CPU.
- Optional upgrade: ElevenLabs eleven_v4 with a stock library voice. It costs about 1,150-1,500 credits (roughly $0.22-0.28) per Short.
Ask what GPU I have. Any GPU works, and a gaming GPU renders a minute of video in about 4 minutes.
Tell me everything else is free: Three.js, Playwright with a headless browser, FFmpeg, faster-whisper, Pixabay music and Mixkit sound effects. No image, video or 3D model generator is used anywhere.
Then write the script and the beat list with seconds, and show me both before you build anything.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1080x1920, 30 fps, 55-75 s vertical Short in the style of the biggest narrated "true story with a twist" Shorts: flat 2D cartoon people acting inside lit, dressed 3D toon sets, one storyteller voice, captions of 1-2 words, and one camera that keeps travelling.

Sets (Three.js 0.170):
- Build one connected world per story from boxes, cylinders, lathes, extrusions and instanced clumps, never a downloaded model. Every place in the story lives in it, joined so the camera can travel between them.
- Materials: MeshToonMaterial on a soft 4-step ramp (168, 206, 236, 255 out of 255), so shadows never go black.
- Ink outlines in #2a2230: a back-faced shell 3.5 cm bigger than each box, or back faces pushed out along the normals for round shapes.
- Draw surfaces on canvas and use them as textures: planks, stone courses, brick, rivets, signs, gravel, rock strata.
- Dress every corner with props. Scatter about 2,000 small clumps of dry grass or small stones near the lens. Open, empty fields read as cheap.
Palette and light:
- Pick each set's two-colour scheme before anything else: a warm key against cool shadows. Examples: a red canyon with purple shadows under a deep blue sky, hot pink against cyan, a navy storm against an amber cabin.
- Balance cream, ochre and amber against blue, teal, purple and mint. Green never leads. Costumes contrast with the set.
- Day:
  - a low golden sun (#ffc27a, strength 2.7) that casts long shadows
  - sky top #2f5fc4, horizon #ffc07e, bottom #8a7ac0
  - fog #f2c49c at density 0.0021
  - a purple hemisphere fill: sky #7a74e0, ground #d89a68, strength 1.15
  - the ground tinted warm (#ffd890)
- Night:
  - deep navy: sky top #081038, horizon #24307a, fog #18225a at density 0.0036
  - fill #5a5ae0 over #283060
  - glowing lamps and lit windows
- Interiors:
  - no sun, warm lamps, a purple fill (#8a7ae0), exposure about 1.25
  - one bold theme colour per room (a green office, teal tiles, a red map room)
  - windows that show a dusk sky
- Sky: a shader dome with a sun glow, a moon and stars. Mix between looks over time, so dawn or night arrives on the words.
- Post, in this order:
  - depth of field from the depth buffer (48 taps, focused on the subject, shallow on close-ups)
  - bloom: strength 0.42, threshold 0.82, radius 0.6
  - Neutral tone mapping at exposure 1.32
  - a split-tone pass:
    - shadows plus RGB (0.03, -0.012, 0.085)
    - highlights plus (0.045, 0.018, -0.035)
    - greens pulled 55% toward gold (hue 0.125)
    - blacks lifted to 0.055 with a purple tint (0.85, 0.75, 1.2)
    - gain 1.08
  - a light grade: saturation 1.08, vignette 0.22, 2% grain
- Targets, measured on 1 frame a second with the caption band left out:
  - mean lightness (Lab L) 43-57
  - darkest 5% at 5-18 (lifted, never crushed)
  - brightest 5% at 88-99
  - shadows purple-blue (Lab a +7 to +19, b 0 to -19)
  - highlights warm (a +3 to +10)
  - blue and purple make up 22-51% of the saturated pixels
People:
- 2D characters are drawn in code on a canvas every frame and shown on camera-facing cards inside the 3D world.
  - Each card's canvas is 512, 1024, 2048 or 3072 px tall, picked by how big the card is on screen, so close-ups stay sharp.
  - A soft blue-violet blob shadow sits under each card.
- About 1.4 m tall, in rig units:
  - a big round head (radius 55)
  - a short bean torso (92-108)
  - long stick legs (132-170)
  - noodle arms (92) with ball hands
  - a 4 px dark outline (#272236)
- A bendy spine (lean, bend, squash), and heads that tilt and turn to three-quarter view (the face slides across the head).
- The face set:
  - dot eyes with angled brows (calm, smug)
  - white circles with dot pupils (shock)
  - closed arcs (laughing)
  - grin, wavy worried mouth, blush, sweat drops
- Pose-to-pose acting: each key snaps in with a small overshoot, then holds, while blinks and breathing keep the holds alive. Bodies act too: they lean in, recoil, slump and point.
- The scene light tints them: an ambient tint, a lit side, a shade colour and a rim (warm gold at dawn, cool blue at night, orange in smoke).
- Each character gets one look built from shared parts: hats, uniforms, moustaches, hair.
Camera:
- No cuts inside a place.
  - One camera holds each beat with a slow push (ease-out), then travels to the next beat.
  - Travels dive down, rise over an edge, fly across, slide through a window, or pan from the clue down to the object.
  - One travel can be a crane up through the sky into a new place or time.
- Travels use a smooth speed ramp (smootherstep) with a slight arc. Only travels get motion blur: 10 subframes over half a frame.
- Never parked: every hold pushes, arcs or slides.
- Low and wide:
  - fov 54-64, with the lens at knee to chest height
  - leading lines (rails, decks, roads) aimed at the subject
  - characters 1-3 m from the lens and leaning in; the mocker gets a big close-up
- Inserts carry the proof: a macro held 3-5 s while the change happens in frame.
- The payoff is a wide, centred spectacle, with the event coming at the lens.
- Hard cuts only for a big jump in place or time: 0-6 per Short.
Captions:
- 1-2 words at a time; short words (a, the, so, to) ride with the next word.
- Montserrat 800 at 76 px, white with a 15 px #120e1a outline and a soft shadow, centred at y 1345.
- Each pops from 108% to 100% in 0.09 s and shows 0.1 s before its word. No full stops on screen.
Banned:
- AI images or video, downloaded 3D models, real logos
- green-on-green sets, crushed blacks
- a camera that sits still, motion blur on holds
- a time-stretched or whispered voice
- more than one name the viewer has to remember
</direction>

<structure>
Length: 55-75 s, 200-280 words. The voice runs about 3.7 words a second, pauses included.
Beat map for a 62 s Short (scale it to your voice):
0-3 s, HOOK, 9-14 words: one plain sentence about an act that makes no sense, with the reason hidden.
- Two things can't both be true, or someone does the opposite of what anyone would do.
- Write it before the rest of the story.
- Picture: the act and the danger in one low, wide frame.
3-12 s, SETUP: present tense, with exact numbers (a price, a time limit, a distance): who, where, and what's at stake. The camera travels across the world to show it.
12-20 s, THE MOCKER: a quoted joke line of 4-12 words, sarcastic and funny, said to the hero's face. Big close-up, leaning into the lens.
20-27 s, THE HERO stays calm and cryptic: one short line, or just a gesture. He never explains.
27-40 s, ESCALATION in threes: it gets weirder, and the mocker gets cocky. A macro insert is held 3-5 s while the change happens. Add one comic aside per beat.
40-52 s, "YOU SEE,": used once, at 60-85% of the runtime. The trick is explained through an everyday thing the viewer has done (blowing on soup, a phone sliding off a table), in 3-5 short lines.
52-62 s, THE PAYOFF: shown, not explained, and it lands on the mocker. The last line is the biggest reveal, with no moral and no trivia after it. The last frame leads back into the first, so it loops.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools (all free): Python 3, Playwright with Edge or Chromium, FFmpeg, faster-whisper, numpy, soundfile, kokoro-onnx, and Three.js 0.170 from npm, loaded with an import map, no bundler. Montserrat comes free from Google Fonts. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Script:
   - Topic: true, one bizarre image you can picture instantly, someone outsmarts someone, and the title hides the ending.
     - Explainers, nature facts and fiction without a trick do far worse.
     - So do topics where a science lesson is the twist.
   - Tell it the way a 10-year-old tells a friend:
     - plain spoken words in flowing sentences joined with "and" and "so"
     - "a captain", "the boss", never titles and dates
     - 0-1 names, no context lines, no jargon
     - one funny comparison
   - Join related sentences with commas, because a voice resets after every full stop and leaves a gap.
   - No cute gags, no "on purpose" spoilers, no low stakes.
   - Study first, free: pull the transcripts of 3 of the newest top Shorts in this format with yt-dlp (--skip-download --write-auto-subs --sub-lang en --sub-format vtt), strip the timestamps, and note how many words each line has, where the mocker speaks and where "You see," lands.
   - Then fill this skeleton line by line, 16-20 lines in all:
     - line 1: the hook, the strange act with the reason hidden, 9-14 words
     - lines 2-4: the setup, who and where, one exact number, what's at stake
     - line 5: the mocker's joke, quoted, 4-12 words
     - line 6: the hero's calm, cryptic reply, or just a gesture
     - lines 7-11: the escalation in threes, each step weirder, the mocker getting cocky, one comic aside
     - lines 12-15: "You see," and the trick told through an everyday thing the viewer has done
     - lines 16-18: the payoff shown and landing on the mocker, the biggest reveal as the very last line
   - Check the finished script line by line against those 3 transcripts before any voice.
   - Show me the word count and the seconds per line.
3. Voice, free first:
   Free route, Kokoro:
   - Run kokoro-onnx on the CPU with the free kokoro-v1.0.onnx model and voices-v1.0.bin, lang en-us.
   - Try 4-5 American male voices (am_puck, am_michael, am_fenrir, am_echo, am_adam) on the first 12 s of the script at speed 1.0-1.1.
   - Keep the voice with the widest pitch range (the gate below).
   - Generate one line per call, so each line gets its own speed: 1.0 for calm lines, 1.1 for excited ones.
   - Join the lines with 0.18 s gaps, and 0.3 s before a big turn.
   - It will sound flatter than a person. Because the film is anchored to the words, you can drop in a better voice later without touching the animation.
   Optional upgrade, ElevenLabs:
   - Use eleven_v4 with a stock library narrator; we used Mark, an energetic young male voice. Never clone a real creator.
   - Put audio tags at the start of lines: [excited], [mischievously], [laughs], [curious], [sarcastically], [chuckles], [dramatically].
   - Put CAPS on one punch word per line ("he did NOTHING", "the ENTIRE town"). An ellipsis gives a beat before a punchline.
   - Never use whisper, soft or sigh tags.
   - Read the whole script in one take at natural speed, and make 4 takes to pick from.
     - A 192-word script came out at 64.6 s for 1,147 credits (about $0.22).
     - We cut pauses over 0.35 s down to 0.28 s (FFmpeg silenceremove at -45 dB) and applied atempo 1.15, which gave 56.0 s.
     - Never go faster than that.
   Gate every take, either route, before building on it:
   - Words a second while talking: 3.5-4.5.
   - Gaps between sentences: median 0.12-0.25 s, longest 0.35 s, none over 0.5 s. Pauses under 13% of the runtime.
   - Pitch range 12.5+ semitones, and pitch movement 11+ semitones a second (pyin over the voiced frames). Under that sounds flat.
   - Stress spread over the line: under 55% of the loud words in each line's first third.
   - Dead air: count the frames 50 dB under the speech peak inside gaps over 0.3 s.
     - Takes with 9-13 s a minute sounded like a robot.
     - 1-4 s a minute of breaths sounded natural.
   - Whispered words: a word with pitch found in under 20% of its frames is whispered.
     - Regenerate just that line and drop it into the pause before the next sentence, never mid-line.
     - Expect 1-2 lines per Short, about 100 credits each.
   - Level to -16 LUFS. Then run faster-whisper on the finished track, without the script as a prompt, to get word times.
4. Film: one HTML page with one canvas, where every frame is a pure function of time: window .seek(t), window.READY, window.END.
   - Align the clean script to the whisper words. A helper T('word', n) returns the start of the nth time that word is said.
   - Anchor every beat, camera hold, pose change, effect and sound event to a T() plus an offset, never a typed time. A new voice then means re-run whisper, re-render and re-mix, nothing else.
   - A world module builds the set and exposes props through simple controls. Give every transformation in the story a 0-to-1 control (setChange(k)) that builds it in visible steps, and use a clipping plane for sweeps like paint or water.
   - A cast module holds the looks and the lights.
   - One rig function draws a character from a pose: lean, bend, squash, facing, turn, head tilt, hands, feet, eyes, brows, mouth, blush, sweat. A keyed(keys, t) helper does the pose-to-pose timing.
   - The camera is a list of holds, each with start, end, position, look-at, [fov from, to], aperture and focus point. The gaps between holds are the travels.
   - window.EV lists the sound events {t, name}, pushed from the same anchors. The renderer saves it for the mix.
5. Style check before the render:
   - Grab 3-4 frames and lay them side by side with frames from 2-3 of the newest Shorts in this format.
   - Render only if palette, shadow colour, lens height and texture match. Measure the colour targets.
   - Make a contact sheet with the first and last frame of every hold. Fix:
     - faces cut off
     - characters inside geometry
     - empty corners
     - captions over faces
     - a camera that starts a cut inside a hill or a wall
6. Render:
   - Headless Edge or Chromium through Playwright seeks every frame. Launch flags: --enable-gpu --ignore-gpu-blocklist --allow-file-access-from-files, plus --use-angle=d3d11 on Windows.
   - The page encodes itself with WebCodecs H.264 on the GPU: 60 Mbps, a keyframe every 2 s. Never read pixels back.
   - Reference speed: 56.2 s = 1,685 frames at 1080x1920, 30 fps, in 3 min 53 s (about 7 fps) on an RTX 3060 Ti with an i5-12400F.
   - The master is about 415 MB. Re-encode with libx264 for upload: 8 Mbps comes to about 57 MB a minute.
7. Glitch scan, on the silent render before the mix:
   - Flag whole-frame jumps that are not planned cuts, one-frame A-B-A flickers, and single blocks that change while their neighbours stay calm (pop-ins, blinks).
   - Look at the frames around each flag and fix the cause. A first cut usually has 10-20.
8. Sound:
   - Music: one playful bed under a free licence (Pixabay). Cut it or drop it on the biggest moment.
   - Ambience: one bed per place, swapped on each cut or crane (distant explosions, waves and birds, night creaks, a cockpit drone).
   - Effects: about 45 Mixkit cues placed from window.EV, so each effect's loudest moment lands on its frame.
     - Whooshes on travels, a pop on reveals, a freeze hit, impacts, a ding on the idea.
     - Big hits go in pauses. Hits that land on words sit under the voice.
   - Duck music and effects about 13 dB under the voice with a sidechain. The music bed sits 20 dB under the narrator.
   - Measure it: mix a voice-only and a background-only version, compare them K-weighted in 0.4 s windows, and fix anything that misses either target:
     - median gap of 15 dB or more
     - background louder than the voice in under 1% of the talking
   - Two-pass loudnorm to -14 LUFS, true peak -1.5.
9. Upload text:
   - Title: "The [thing] That [strange act]" or "Why [something odd]", hiding the ending. No emoji, no hashtags; the description is the title.
   - Cover: a clean frame of the payoff with no text.
   - Made for kids: No.
</build>

<gotchas>
Script:
- The first scripts read like writing: names, dates, history context, the twist given away in the hook, no doubters, an ending that fizzled. They were rejected.
  - Rewritten the way a 10-year-old tells it, with a mocker and the reveal saved for the end, they worked.
  - Count names and context lines; a reading-level score doesn't catch this.
- A 121-word script had no room to escalate. The biggest Shorts in this format run 145-295 words, and the newest ones 218-295.
- An opener that is setup ("During a war...") or gives the answer away kills curiosity. Line 1 is the strange act with the reason hidden.
Voice:
- Short full-stop sentences make every voice reset with a 0.5-0.85 s gap and punch the next first word, so it sounds stop-start. Join lines with commas.
- A time-stretch (1.15) on top of pauses cut to 0.18 s got "did you speed it up?", and cutting breaths out sounds robotic. Speed comes from the script, not the edit.
- Whisper or relieved tags made the narrator whisper a whole line. Leave them out.
- Kokoro was rejected as a final voice for sounding flat, but it is a fine free start: build on it, then swap the voice when you can.
- Whisper given the script as its prompt garbled the transcript. Run it without one.
- Anchor repeated words by occurrence ("so" number 3), or beats land on the wrong line.
Look:
- Olive people on olive vehicles on bright grass under a pale sky read as cheap. Pick a warm-against-cool scheme first; green never leads.
- Using the grade isn't enough. One Short with ochre walls, an orange road and warm shadows drifted all orange. Pale interiors went flat.
  - Set palette and interior light decide the look, so check frames side by side every time.
- The colour metric's "warm" bin counts pink-purple (hue over 300). Trust the side-by-side over that number.
Camera:
- 17 cuts in 35 s, a fixed 1 s cut grid, whips, shakes and blur everywhere read as glitchy visuals unrelated to the voice. Hold, push, travel; cut only for a jump in place or time.
- A camera at eye level, mid-distance, at fov 36-46 felt lazy and flat. Low, wide and close felt right.
- Hermite camera keys overshoot when a neighbouring key is far away, and the camera flies through walls.
  - Use eased travels (smootherstep) or centripetal Catmull-Rom splines with arc-length speed.
- A camera key inside geometry renders black. A fast travel through a pole, a wall or an actor reads as a glitch. Make those hard cuts.
- A long travel at street level smears through shopfronts. Cut for big jumps inside a town.
- The portrait frame is only about 23 degrees wide at fov 40. Keep characters within a few degrees of the look line.
  - Turn actors three-quarter to camera, or a raised far arm hides behind the big head.
Render:
- Characters vanish inside other geometry: a hill mesh swallows anyone standing inside its radius, and foliage clumps swallow heads.
  - Keep people on clear ground.
  - Open a sight line through foliage between the camera and what it looks at: 9 m long at most, faded in over 4 m so the clumps don't jump.
- An InstancedMesh whose count or matrices change after the first frame keeps its first bounding sphere and gets culled, so leaves blinked. Set frustumCulled = false.
- Transparent planes with the same renderOrder at the same height swap draw order as the camera moves, so they flicker. Give each its own order.
- Culling character cards with fixed screen margins makes close-ups pop in at the frame edges. Scale the margin with the card's size.
- Pose fields set outside the key system snap. Ease every change. Give props to a hand instead of switching them on with a pose.
- Effects that outlive a cut show up in the next shot: a splash from one shot hangs as a ghost over a face in the next. End them at the cut.
- A camera near plane of 0.05 loses flat effects near the ground to the depth test in a band at the bottom of some frames. Use 0.3.
  - Check stills at exact frame times (frame / 30), not rounded ones.
- Motion blur on holds ghosts the captions at every word change. Blur travels only.
- Reading pixels back every frame (toDataURL, screenshots) knocks the canvas off the GPU and renders about 50x slower. Encode inside the page.
Sound:
- With the music only 7-9 dB under the voice, the narrator was hard to hear. Duck it and measure before you export.
- A voice already hitting the peak cap can't go louder. Pull everything else down instead.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for my story, or pitch 3. Then show me the script (word count and seconds per line) and the beat list before any voice is generated or any scene is built.
</start>

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku and Opus 5.5 together, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Opus-level judgment on every big call, without paying Opus rates for every routine turn.

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

→ Haiku 5.5 explores files and docs in parallel

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku explores. Opus reviews.

X just silently updated its open-source algorithm.

Two massive shifts just happened in the code:

1. Clickbait is officially dying (taps dropped again).
2. AI replies under big accounts now get flagged as "llm slop" and muted from notifications.

I ran the Nov 5 code update through Claude. Here is what changed and how small accounts can exploit it:

📊 The New Weights (Nov 5 Update)

What’s UP:
📈 Likes: 0.66 → 0.708 (Up +41% since early October)
📈 Time Spent: 0.006 → 0.0075 (Up +25% in a week, nearly 2x since Oct)
📈 Shares: 2.0 → 2.118

What’s DOWN:
📉 Tapping a post: 0.30 → 0.274
📉 10s+ stay after tap: 0.40 → 0.385
📉 Opening a video: 0.02 → 0.00 (Dead)
📉 "Not interested" penalty: -52.27 → -53.07

The takeaway: A tap isn't the win anymore. Retention + Likes is the new meta. Write to be read to the very last line.

🤖 The "LLM Slop" Rule (Crucial for Reply Guys)

X runs an automated check on replies under accounts with 250K+ followers.

• If your reply smells like ChatGPT, you get hit with a literal "llm slop" label for 14 to 30 days.
• New rule: Once labeled, your replies and mentions will NOT reach their notifications (unless they already follow you).
• Big/credible accounts bypass this. Small accounts don't. Write your own replies or stay invisible.

🎥 Video & Profile Retention

Why did "opening a video" drop to 0? Because X turned on two new ranking signals:

1. Video watch time after opening.
2. Profile dwell time after someone clicks your name.

Hook viewers in the first 2 seconds (videos must be 10s+ to rank), and optimize your bio/pinned post so people stick around when they visit.

⚡ The Ultimate X Playbook (What still works right now)

1. The Golden Window (First 2 Hours)
• Your post gets a boost during its first 2 hours and first 200 views. Post when your audience is awake.
• The 1st like and the 32nd like unlock new distribution tiers.
• Originals from accounts under 50K can jump straight to spot #16 on feeds if early viewers hit like.
• Don't double-post quickly: your 2nd post in the same feed gets throttled to 62% reach.

2. The Real Multiplier Scores
• Copy Link: +20 points (Still the king of metrics)
• Mutual back-and-forth in replies: +20 points (Engage with friends!)
• Quotes, Replies, DM Shares: +5 points each
• Likely to earn a follow: +4 points
• Bookmarks: 0 points (They don't boost reach alone, only the time spent reading does)

3. Instant Reach Killers to Avoid
🚫 Off-topic posts: One "Not interested" click costs you -53.07 points.
🚫 Bad link in Pinned Post: Linking to a low-trust domain in your pin can shadow-label your whole account for 7 days.
🚫 Spamming replies under 1 post: Piling multiple replies under a big account tanks your score.
🚫 Self-plagiarism: Reusing your exact old tweets triggers a "copypasta" flag.
🚫 Relying on Replies/RTs for growth: Non-followers are only shown your original posts in For You.

holy f*ck... the best AI agents don't have a better model. they have better notes

Stanford University just published the whole method for free in a paper called Agentic Context Engineering. your agent reviews every run, writes down each lesson and adds it to its notes. it never rewrites them, so nothing it learns is ever lost

same weights, zero fine-tuning. 38.6% → 64.2%, level with IBM's top production agent on Opus 5.5. fine-tuning for that jump costs $5,000-20,000. here it cost $0

it comes down to 4 agents:

→ worker: does the task and saves the full log
→ critic: reads the log and marks every mistake and every win
→ teacher: turns each one into a one-line lesson
→ librarian: files the lesson into CLAUDE.md. merges duplicates, never deletes a line

that's why asking your agent to "clean up" your CLAUDE.md is a mistake. every rewrite throws away lessons it already paid for

paste this into Claude Code:

"Run 4 agents on my last 10 sessions in ~/.claude/projects. Critic: mark every mistake and every win. Teacher: turn each one into a one-line lesson, what happened and what to do next time. Librarian: add only new lessons to my CLAUDE.md under ## Lessons, merge exact duplicates, never rewrite or delete an existing line. Worker: rerun 2 of the failed tasks with the new lessons and save the full log. Show me the diff and both results before saving"
