I'm going to give a contrarian take on Neoclouds like $NBIS and say the theme looks compelling after the valuation crash. 

Since there's a reason why Elon's $SPCX is heavily focused on this market full of "guppies" that would die: 

He sees how attractive the economics are after selling compute to $GOOGL and Anthropic. 

And this is reflected by his actions not words, from SpaceX's recent $40B financing for GPUs procurement. 
$AMZN, $MSFT, and even $META also see how profitable the economics are and are accelerating their AI DC buildouts. 

I'd argue if a Neocloud has: 

- Close relationships with $NVDA + others for allocations
- Existing contracted capacity + permitting
- Well funded counterparties, such as Hyperscalers. 
- Attractive economics, such as financing their procurement correctly (not the way $CRWV has with high debt interest unless they refinance). 

Then I think they'll do just fine... 

However, the bigger worry is more toward newer players starting financing or the permitting process, since barrier to entry has now become extremely high. 

For financing, read through on $IREN earnings has shown public Neoclouds can adapt extremely well to tight markets:

As seen with their 90% prepayments for GPU capex on a 5Y deal. 

Their older H100 GPUs recontracted at double their previous pricing and 12% higher contracted pricing also point against depreciation fears. 

And in the case DC buildouts slow from permitting delays... it heavily favors some over others. 

Rosenblatt's recent note for example stated they see little risk with $NBIS primary buildout that was in Missouri, Pennsylvania, and South Carolina. 

And there's probably less risk with developers in places like Australia. 

Markets have also show this infinite compute arbitrage can't go on forever, hence the reluctance to further finance capex, via things like ATMs. 

But ironically, tighter financing and hypothetical restrictive permitting would increase the competitive advantage of established neoclouds. 

And create a larger moat against newer DC developers.

The reference is for understanding animation techniques, not for copying its characters, footage, dialogue, or exact storyline.

The reference runs approximately 50 seconds at 1080×1920 and 60 FPS.

2D blocky Roblox-inspired cartoon characters

Clean dark outlines around characters and objects
Simple geometric bodies
Large square or rounded-square heads

Other available text-to-speech service

Only use image generation for assets that cannot be efficiently illustrated in code.

<STEP 3 — SCRIPT STRUCTURE>

Write an original 45–55 second script.

Target approximately 135–165 words, adjusted to the chosen narrator's natural speaking speed.

The storytelling must feel fast, funny, and unpredictable.

Use short sentences.

Make every sentence introduce an action, joke, reveal, or consequence.

Avoid lengthy explanations.

STORY FORMULA

0–3 seconds — THE HOOK

Open with an absurd Roblox-related situation.

Example:

"What if your dad gave you just TEN seconds to become the richest player in Roblox?"

Show the situation immediately.

No intro sequence.

No logos.

No slow setup.

3–8 seconds — THE RULES

Introduce the challenge or restriction.

Show the protagonist reacting.

Use an animated timer, warning, or game mechanic to create urgency.

8–15 seconds — THE FIRST WIN

The main character starts making progress.

Show an entertaining action sequence.

Introduce the first reward, achievement, or surprise.

15–24 seconds — ESCALATION

Increase the stakes.

Add something visually ridiculous:

Massive rewards

A difficult obstacle course

A giant enemy

A strange transformation
An unexpected purchase
A character gaining an absurd ability
Each new event should be more surprising than the previous one.

The protagonist's advantage creates a new challenge.

Use exaggerated character reactions.

33–43 seconds — COUNTDOWN AND PANIC

Increase the urgency.

Show the character trying to solve the problem.

Use faster cuts, close-ups, ticking sounds, and a changing timer.

43–50 seconds — COMEDIC PAYOFF

Deliver an unexpected outcome that connects to the opening situation.

50–55 seconds — LOOPABLE ENDING

End with a funny final line, cliffhanger, or question.

Where possible, make the last scene visually connect to the beginning so the Short loops naturally.

Every line must be visually actionable.

Do not write narration that cannot be shown through animation.

The protagonist should have a clear objective.

The story needs at least one surprise and one comedic payoff.

Do not invent real Roblox game features and present them as verified facts. Fictional powers and game mechanics are allowed when clearly part of the story.

Provide the complete script for approval.

Aspect ratio: 9:16

Frame rate: 60 FPS

Format: MP4

Stylized lighting
Recognizable game-inspired objects

THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 at once, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

Finally. I called it months ago.

I have been saying for months that SpaceX is the Kingmaker in AI and that SpaceX gets to decide who wins and loses in the AI race.

Yesterday @chamath basically comes to the same conclusion in the All In Podcast.

“Chamath on SpaceX and Anthropic:
Their compute deal has a mutual 90-day out. Either side can walk away.
And he says Elon ending it would be "the king-making move, because if Elon pulls it and reprices at spot, his guess is 2-3x the revenue instantly on the Anthropic deal”

Ok so here are my thoughts

Chamath says SpaceX can walk away from its compute deal with Anthropic in 90 days. Most people heard a contract detail. I heard who holds the power in AI.

Money isn't the thing anymore. Compute is. It's already happening. People don't want to be paid in dollars, they want to be paid in compute. Because you can't buy what doesn't exist yet.

Now look at Anthropic. They can't not buy compute. They need every bit they can get, and the shortage runs for years. Walking away isn't an option.

Now look at SpaceX. SpaceX has its own AI too, Grok Bot, and it's also short on compute. So every GW SpaceX builds has two choices. Sell it, or use it themselves. Either way they win.

And they can build it faster than anyone. Rockets, Starlink, power, orbit. Everyone else only owns a piece of the stack. Chips, or models, or data centers. SpaceX owns all of it. Full flexibility, full power.

My guess: in 2 years SpaceX is the biggest compute dealer on earth. And in space they'd have it to themselves.

That's what a kingmaker is. Not the one who wins the AI race. The one who decides who gets to run in it.

And they never have to cancel anything. The threat is enough. Every lab knows the supply could go somewhere else, so every lab stays friendly.

Now the deepest part. Compute = intelligence. Enough intelligence is ASI. And ASI can disrupt anything. Every industry, every job, every market.

So what is compute really worth? Not what it costs to build. What it unlocks.

That's why I think the spot price of compute only goes one way from here. Up. The company that controls the most of it controls the future.

this is f*cking INSANE... citadel & two sigma quants basically LEAKED their hedge fund stack on gitHub

zipline’s #1 author now runs equities engineering at Citadel, and pandas was led for years by a Two Sigma managing director

They’re called zipline, pandas and Lightweight Charts, and they already have 88,500+ GitHub stars together

First, get how it works:

1. zipline is “a Pythonic algorithmic trading library”, “an event-driven system for backtesting”, the engine that ran Quantopian’s crowd-sourced hedge fund

2. pandas gives you “fast, flexible, and expressive data structures”: every price, signal and P&L of the backtest lives in its DataFrames

3. Lightweight Charts is TradingView’s own chart engine, “one of the smallest and fastest financial HTML5 charts”, so every trade lands on your screen

Here’s how you can run it for free yourself:

1. Install Claude Code: npm install -g @ anthropic-ai/claude-code, open a new folder and run claude

2. Ask it to install the stack: pip install zipline-reloaded pandas

3. Tell Claude Code: “download BTC/USD daily candles from Kraken’s public API and save them as a CSV”

4. Ask it to register the CSV as a zipline bundle on a 24/7 calendar and run zipline ingest -b btc

5. Tell Claude Code: “write a zipline strategy for BTC with a trend signal, a stop and a target”

6. Backtest it: zipline run -f strategy. py --start 2024-1-1 --end 2025-12-31 -b btc -o results.pickle

7. Ask Claude Code to open results.pickle with pandas and print the returns, the drawdown and every trade

8. Build your chart screen: npm install --save lightweight-charts, then a page that draws the candles, entries and exits

9. Put it on your big monitor, and let Claude Code rerun the backtest every time you change the strategy

i killed the infographics show with 1 claude opus prompt

now i made a full 10 minute story video in full code

this cost me $0 in ai video generations btw

turned it into a prompt you can use for free and make any topic u want, enjoy ↓

<inputs>
Ask me for my topic and my script. If I have no script, write one from my topic.
Ask which image model I have: GPT Image 2, or any model that takes reference images at 2K-4K, at about $0.03-0.05 an image.
Ask which voice I have: ElevenLabs, or Kokoro for free.
Before generating everything, show me a look test: one plate, one character sheet cut out and rigged, and a 10 s shot with typing, a tag and a character who talks and points. Wait for my OK.
</inputs>

<look>
A 1920x1080 animated explainer in the style of the big flat-vector infographic channels.
- Every line of narration is acted out by cartoon people inside a full illustrated place.
- All motion is code. There are no AI video generations, just a few still images that code cuts up, rigs and animates.

Art:
- Flat colour shapes with NO outlines, at most one slightly darker flat shade for form, simple geometric shapes and crisp edges.
- Muted palette: dusty blue-grey, slate teal, warm beige, navy, soft purple. Salmon-pink skin, big round heads, dot eyes, small bodies.
- Mood comes from the plate's own light: daylight, a cold blue night, warm indoor lamps.

Code colours:
- ink #2b2d42, red #d62828, orange #f4a261, gold #f6b93b, green #2fb37a, navy #1f2a48
- headline tomato #e2552f and purple #5b3fa6
- grey labels #8a8c9c, white cards #ffffff
- Font: Montserrat 800-900 (Google Fonts), all caps on cards and signs.

Pace:
- A new place every 3-4 s, about 10 places a minute.
- Something new arrives every 2 s: a tag, a stamp, a person walking in, a number.
- Never hold a still over 1 s. Never have a character who doesn't move.

Banned:
- outlines, glossy UI panels floating over the art, emoji, burned-in subtitles
- any channel's logo or name, photos of real people
- facts written on a plain colour card when the place could hold them
</look>

<art>
About 60 images in all ($2-3).

Every prompt starts with this style core, word for word:
"Flat vector illustration in exactly the same art style as the reference images: NO outlines or line art anywhere, every shape is a flat solid colour fill with at most one slightly darker flat shade for form, simple geometric shapes, crisp clean edges, no gradients, no texture, no painterly lighting. Muted modern palette: dusty blue-grey, slate teal, warm beige, navy, soft purple, salmon-pink skin. No text, no letters, no numbers, no logos."

Then add one line that locks the setting ("The setting is [time, place]: [materials, light sources], nothing from other eras unless asked"). Feed 3-5 frames of a reference channel in as style references, with their logo cropped off.

1. Hero plates, about 24, one full 16:9 image each, for places you zoom into or come back to.
   - EMPTY: "no people, no characters, no animals".
   - Straight-on, with an open floor in the middle where characters will stand.
   - Blank signs, boards, screens and pages that code writes on later.
2. Quad plates, about 19, giving 76 more places. Pack 4 places into one image:
   "The image is a 2x2 grid of FOUR completely separate scenes, each filling exactly one quarter of the image (each quarter is itself a 16:9 picture), divided by perfectly straight thin pure-white gutters, one vertical down the exact centre and one horizontal across the exact centre."
   - Then describe the TOP-LEFT, TOP-RIGHT, BOTTOM-LEFT and BOTTOM-RIGHT scenes.
   - Split each quad on the brightest white row and column near the centre, walk out while the line stays over 60% white, and trim 6 px more.
   - Crop each tile to 16:9 at 1920x1080.
   - Object close-ups make great tiles: a desk, a screen, a document, a plate of food, a vault.
3. Main characters, 2-3 of them. Write one fixed description per character (age, hair, face, every piece of clothing with colours) and paste it word for word into every sheet.
   - Base sheet: 6 views. (1) front, neutral, drawn WITHOUT ARMS, only round smooth shoulder sockets where the arms would join; (2) the same armless front with a second emotion; (3) side view walking right; (4) seen from behind; (5) and (6) two poses the script needs.
   - Expression sheet: 6 armless fronts (hopeful, disgusted, terrified, exhausted, sick, shocked, or whatever the script needs), with the base sheet as a reference.
   - Pose sheet: 6 full poses with their props (sitting at a desk typing, sleeping, eating, running, signing, falling), with the base sheet as a reference.
4. Everyone else: role sheets of 4-6 people, each drawn in the exact pose their shot needs; crowd sheets of 8-10 small figures; prop sheets.
   - Every sheet: "on a solid flat chroma green background (#00B140) with lots of empty green space between figures; nothing touches, nothing on any character or object is green, full bodies, nothing cut off by the edges".
5. Thumbnail art: the same characters with richer saturated cartoon lighting and extreme emotions, the top quarter left free, no text, with the base sheets as references.
</art>

<rig>
Cutouts:
- The background is every border-connected pixel with G - max(R,B) over 40 and within 110 of the median green. Key only from the border, or dark clothes leak.
- Add a 2 px soft alpha band and clamp G to max(R,B) + 6 inside it, which kills the green fringe.
- Group the pieces by figure and drop specks. Name every sprite, and show me a named contact sheet.

Armless front figures become puppets:
- Split the head at the neck: the narrowest alpha row under the head.
- Find both shoulder sockets and the eye boxes.
- Inpaint the hole under the head from the body's own colours, so a nod never shows a gap.
- Write everything to rig.js: size, neck, sockets, eye boxes, skin RGB, sleeve RGB.
- Arms: upper L1 about 0.13 of the figure's height, lower L2 about 0.12, thickness about 0.04. Use sleeve colour to the elbow and skin for the forearm, a 0.82x darker sleeve when the arm is behind the body, and round caps and joins.
- Hands: mittens in three shapes (mitt, open, fist), plus a point with one finger out.
- Arm poses: each is a hand target relative to its shoulder, in units of L = L1 + L2, solved by two-bone IK (where there are two signs, the first is the left arm).
  - down: (∓0.04, 0.97)
  - rest: (±0.1, 0.9)
  - hips: (∓0.42, 0.55) with fists
  - point: right hand to (0.86, -0.32)
  - present: right hand to (0.75, 0.25), open
  - shrug: (∓0.62, 0.12), open
  - up: (∓0.32, -0.9)
  - hands on head
  - chin: a fist at the neck
  - hold: (±0.42, 0.45)
  - wave: (0.5, -0.75)
  - stop: (0.55, -0.1)
  - cheer: (∓0.55, -0.75) with fists
  - A pose change blends the two targets over 0.3-0.5 s with ease-in-out.
- Side, back and pose sprites stay whole images. Only the head turns, and a drawing or typing hand jitters ±6 px.
</rig>

<animation>
One HTML canvas where every frame is a pure function of time t: window .seek(t), READY, END, and EV, a list of sound events by name.
- Hang every shot on the narration: S('exact words', fn) starts a shot 0.08 s before that phrase. Repeated words are looked up by occurrence number.
- One function per shot, one shots file per chapter.

Motion primitives (Δ = t - start):
- pop: 0.3 s back-ease overshoot, 1 + 2.9(p-1)^3 + 1.9(p-1)^2.
- spring in: 1 - e^(-6.5Δ) cos(13Δ).
- kick on impact: 1 + 0.1 e^(-10Δ) cos(22Δ).
- shake: x = A e^(-8Δ) sin(61Δ), y = A e^(-8Δ) cos(47Δ).
- Exits shrink with ease-in over 0.25 s. Things arrive with a spring, a squash or a white puff, never a plain fade.

Camera:
- camP(plate, zoom, fx, fy) keeps the view inside the plate's edges.
- Every shot moves from one [zoom, fx, fy] to another with ease-in-out, a 2-4% push or a slow pan, so nothing holds still.
- Draw the plate and everything on it inside the same camera transform.
- Keep zoom under 1.33x on quad tiles. Zoom deeper only on hero plates.

Transitions:
- Push: the old shot slides out left while the new one slides in from the right, 0.24 s ease-in-out, with a whoosh 0.02 s before.
- Chapter splat: a #f4f1fb blob covers the screen in 0.2 s and clears in 0.2 s. It's a 1,250 px circle, 12 big satellite blobs at golden-angle spacing and 10 small droplets further out, shifted 120 px left on the way in and 140 px right on the way out.

Characters, alive in every frame:
- Breathing: scale 1 + 0.009 sin(2.3t).
- Head nod: 0.025 sin(2.1t) rad, or 0.025 sin(7t) + 0.02 sin(11.3t) while that character's line is spoken.
- Blink: every 2.7-4.2 s, seeded per figure. For 0.14 s, paint each eye box over in skin colour with a curved lash line.
- Walk:
  - Bob |sin| at 2.2% of the figure's height, with a body rock of ±0.035 rad.
  - Side-view walk sprites slide 1.5 leg lengths per step cycle, so the feet don't skate.
- Enter on the spring, sometimes with a hop. Fear is a fast shake (sin 70t). Surprise is a jump and an orange "!".
- A soft contact shadow ellipse under every figure. Night shots darken them with brightness(1 - k), so they match the plate.
- Every character on screen acts on its line: points at the thing being named, presents it, shrugs, cheers, holds its head.
</animation>

<graphics>
Text only lives on things in the world, typed letter by letter: 28 letters a second (34 for short tags). Each letter starts 1.45x big and 0.7 em to the right and settles in 0.18 s with ease-out.

The full kit:
- Board: a white rounded board (radius 20) that drops 420 px on the spring and swings 0.25 rad into place, or stands on a wooden post and swings up from -1 rad.
  - Soft drop shadow (blur 22, y 8, 22%) and a faint darker strip along its bottom edge.
  - Lines typed 0.3 s apart.
- Date card: top left at (70, 70), white, 120 px tall, at least 330 px wide, radius 18. An orange calendar icon, a grey "DATE:" at 26 px, the date typed at 44 px weight 900. Pops in over 0.32 s.
- Place card: the same card with a red map pin and "PLACE:".
- Tag: a 6 px line with a dot at the thing, drawn in 0.2 s, then a rounded pill (the text at 40 px weight 900) pops on its end. Ink, red, gold or orange pills.
- Number card: a white card with a small grey label and a big red number. Long numbers roll up like a counter with ease-out.
- Red X: two round 30 px strokes, 0.11 s each, 0.01 s apart, with a soft shadow. One goes over every wrong idea.
- Stamp: red text in a double rounded border, tilted -0.12 rad. It slams from 2.1x to 1x in 0.14 s, then kicks.
- Banner: a full-width headline band, 92 px white caps on tomato or purple, rotated -0.02 rad, sliding in from the left over 0.22 s.
- Speech bubble: white, radius 36, with a tail. Thought cloud: a pill with two small circles.
- Orange "?" that bobs and sways over a puzzled head, and an orange "!" pop.
- White puff and poof clouds, speed lines, light blue sweat drops, coins and bills, a soft vignette, and a colour tint for mood.
- Write on the plate's own blank boards, screens and pages whenever the place has them. Measure the blank's rectangle on a grid overlay of the plate first.
</graphics>

<voice>
- ElevenLabs: a deep, warm US documentary narrator, eleven_v4, stability 0.5, similarity 0.75, style 0, speaker boost, with the timestamps endpoint.
- About 170-180 words a minute, using the voice's own speed setting (1.0-1.1). Never speed it up with atempo: it sounds chipmunked.
- Long scripts go in 3 chunks split at chapter breaks, passing the previous and next text so the read stays continuous.
- Cut pauses over 0.24 s to 0.16 s, leave 0.5 s at chapter breaks, and add a 0.3 s lead-in.
- Rebuild word times from the alignment into words.js.
- Run faster-whisper over the result and diff it against the script before building the picture.
- Free route: Kokoro, then faster-whisper for the word times.
</voice>

<sound>
- Music: 2-3 free documentary beds from Pixabay, crossfaded over 3 s at big beats.
- Duck the music under the voice (30 ms attack, 0.3 s hold, 0.45 s release) and let it swell back up between chapters.
- SFX from Mixkit, one per event, aligned by their peaks, 6 dB quieter on speech: a typewriter tick on typing, a whoosh on pushes and splats, a pop on tags and cards, a thud on stamps, a hit on every red X, a ding on ticks, plus sounds that fit the scene.
- Gate: during speech the voice sits 15+ dB over music plus SFX (median of 100 ms frames), and the background is louder than the voice in under 1% of frames.
- Two-pass loudnorm to -14 LUFS, true peak -1 dB.
</sound>

<build>
1. Tools: Python, Playwright with Chromium or Edge, FFmpeg, faster-whisper, OpenCV, Pillow, numpy. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Order:
   - the look test
   - the art in batches, with a contact sheet after each
   - cutouts and rig
   - voice and word times
   - shots, chapter by chapter
3. Check before any full render: a contact sheet per chapter, one frame every 2 s. Fix:
   - empty or overflowing signs
   - text over a face
   - black plate edges
   - feet floating off the floor
   - two shots in a row in the same place
   - any 4 s where nothing new arrives
4. Render at 30 fps, 4 motion-blur subframes over half a frame, frames piped to libx264 CRF 16-18.
   - Split long videos across 4-6 parallel browser pages and join the parts.
   - Scan the result for single-frame jumps and check that each one is a planned cut.
</build>

<gotchas>
- Too few places reads as lazy. One plate held for 30 s with cards over it looks cheap. Budget about 10 new places a minute.
- Some image models ignore "no arms". GPT Image 2 follows it.
- Paste the same character description into every sheet and feed the base sheet back in, or faces and clothes drift.
- Quad tiles are only about 1920 px wide. Pushing past 1.33x looks soft.
- Plates with people already drawn in can't be animated. Ask for EMPTY and check before cutting.
- Text on a card floating over the art looks like a slideshow. Write on the world.
- Long renders crash. Render in parts you can rerun, and back up the shot files before every big patch.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for my topic, my script, my image model and my voice, then make the look test.
</start>

Nobody has ever explained all of Claude to you.

But here's everything about Claude you must know:

Level 1. Don't be lazy, use the Claude desktop app.

You will still use the browser 90% of the time, and that's fine. But the day you start using the Claude desktop app, you'd be able to work with your folders without ever uploading the files one by one. You'd use Claude code more. There is no coming back from there.

Level 2. You have better things to do than spending 1 minute choosing the best model.

Default should be: Opus 5.5 on high. That's it.

Do not switch the models mid-chat. It consumes more tokens because Claude re-reads the entire chat (again) to get the context.

Level 3. Either Medium or High effort. Nothing else

Medium when it is low-effort work. High for most of the tasks. But Extra High mostly burn through your usage limit.

Level 4. Delete your old Claude setup.

Delete the “Instructions for Claude” box in settings. Delete the old added Claude skills. Old skills and prompts might be slowing you down since they were written for old models. Instead, give one goal and end prompts with: “Before you start, restate my goal in your own words.”

Level 5. Ask for HTML. Not for a document.

Add two things to your prompt: “Make it an HTML page” and “for [who will read it].”

Claude will code the image, doc, or any other format. There is no scope of making mistakes.

Level 6. Protect what you plug in.

Never click the thumbs up or down under an answer. You are basically giving feedback to AI, and they are allowed to send it to their training data. On a Team plan, once memory is on, leave it on: if an owner turns it off, every member’s memories are deleted permanently.

Your first 20 minutes, in order:

1. Install desktop app.
2. No settings are the best.
3. Connect ONE tool - not everything.
4. Use Claude Code more than you do.
5. Delete the installed skills, and add the new ones (written for the latest models)
6. Go to https://t.co/cn6xDN1uAS for my Claude skill library.

AI Concierge is one of the best ways to make money as an AI consultant right now.

I'm making over $1,000 per hour as an AI Concierge (99% profit) following this super simple playbook:

1. I like to start with an AI Opportunity Assessment. I spend 60ish minutes interviewing the client to figure out where AI fits into their biz. This is the roadmap we follow during our Concierge engagement.

2. We then book 2 45-60min Zoom calls a month. The client shares their screen and I help them turn their manual processes into Claude skills.

3. I run a framework called AOA for each skill build. We start by Auditing the manual process. Then we Optimize by cutting the steps that shouldn't exist. Lastly, we Automate by turning the new clean process into a skill.

4. In between calls I communicate with clients async via Voxer (a free walkie talkie app). I promise them a 12-business hour response time. I typically reply in under an hour in an attempt to overdeliver.

5. The client gets access to a shared Notion database where I log everything we build/optimize together. Then one of my own Claude skills reads their database and sends them updates after each call on what we accomplished.

The Notion hub is huge for retention because it shows the client in plain English exactly what we accomplished on each call, exactly what was automated, time saved, etc.

I'm basically being paid to identify a client's bottlenecks, help them clean up the process, then turn them into Claude skills.

If you're proficient with Claude (or ChatGPT) then this is a business model you can make great money with at extremely high margins.
